source.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Tatsuro Inaba; Go Kamoda; Kentaro Inui; Masaru Isonuma; Yusuke Miyao; Yohei Oseki; Yu Takagi; Benjamin Heinzerling

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes SAE-recovered features in English-Japanese LLMs across training stages, layers, and model sizes, extending feature-analysis evidence to a bilingual LLM setting. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures SAE feature activation and language/semantic properties in LLMs, bearing on V4. Its intervention results measure the effect of adding decomposed representations on model performance, not whether the claim versions' predicted natural representations occur; those results are recorded under fits_no_version. Toy Models of Superposition is cited in related work, but its method and geometry are not reproduced.
record.test_reason: The study uses TopK-SAEs as a tool to trace English-Japanese language selectivity and semantic coherence across checkpoints, layers and model sizes. It cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background. It never tests whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, or recoverable by SAEs. It does not compare SAE features to neurons, measure reconstruction or feature counts against dimensions, or probe capacity. Its monosemanticity score measures semantic coherence of SAE-feature activating tokens, which is a different construct. The rows are therefore unlinked from all versions, and the findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: models first learn languages separately, then form bilingual alignments, especially in mid layers and larger models. Injecting bilingual representations from the trained model into a mid-training model improves its performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses TopK-SAE feature analysis and activation interventions in bilingual LLMs, rather than the original toy-network setup and feature-geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with layer, training stage, and model size. The intervention study also varies α and m, but its reported ablation table is not extracted here because those induced performance changes do not measure a listed claim version.

fits_no_version.finding: In LLM-jp models, SAE features at a mid layer start mixed-language with low monosemanticity. They then become language-specific and coherent, then bilingual and coherent late in training. Mid layers and larger models show more bilingual alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bilingual LMs first learn language-specific SAE-decomposable features, then form cross-lingual (bilingual) features, more so in mid layers and larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Injecting bilingual SAE-decomposed representations from the final model into a 40B-token checkpoint lowers perplexity in both languages more than monolingual injections. For example, overall PPL drops from 22.43 to 21.96 vs 22.28 for English-specific injection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Injecting bilingual SAE-decomposed representations from a fully trained model improves a mid-training model's bilingual performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors note that SAE interpretability and reliability have been questioned and that reconstruction accuracy is imperfect, so their analysis approximates the model's representations. The study focuses on English and Japanese and cautions that results may not generalize to other language pairs. It reports five-run averages for interventions without uncertainty estimates. Much of the layer- and size-wise evidence is presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Specific plotted values and layer-by-layer outcomes not stated in the text were not reconstructed from Figures 5–9 and 12–17. Figure 3–4 and the textual summaries of Figures 5–9 are represented where the prose gives explicit findings. The Table 4 α and m ablation outcomes are omitted because they report induced intervention performance rather than a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No toy models, feature/dimension sweeps, sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity arising from capacity competition. The vocabulary-vs-SAE-width remark is speculative and concerns SAE features.
No analysis of neuron polysemanticity origins.
No measure of features spread across neurons, and no test that SAEs recover sparse features beyond using them as a tool. Reconstruction quality is not reported quantitatively.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability or canonicity. Authors note imperfect reconstruction.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition is invoked only as motivation for using SAEs. The monosemanticity metric (1 − semantic/token entropy over activating tokens) applies to SAE features, not neurons. It is not evidence about superposition. Intervention rows (R12–R26) are induced performance changes and are correctly unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.

The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from feature competition for limited network capacity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions. Its discussion of vocabulary size exceeding SAE hidden dimension n concerns SAE features and is not a test of this version.
The study analyzes SAE features rather than testing whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.

It studies SAE features in English-Japanese models from one model family; it does not establish that features are spread across neurons generally or that SAE dictionaries recover all relevant features.
It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units. The authors note imperfect reconstruction and interpretability concerns.
It does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: early training, ≤ 4 × 10^8 tokens
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity using SAE features.
rows.value: Most features were categorized as mixed and exhibited low monosemanticity.
rows.note: The authors describe the early activations as lacking consistent semantic or linguistic patterns.
rows.check: Measures language mix and token-semantic coherence of SAE features over training. Does not bear on whether LLMs superpose features or whether SAEs recover them.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: middle training, 4 × 10^8–4 × 10^9 tokens
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity using SAE features.
rows.value: Mixed-language proportion sharply declined and monosemanticity markedly increased.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as features becoming more language-specific and semantically coherent.
rows.check: Same construct as R1 (language specialization of SAE features); not a test of V4.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: late training, ≥ 4 × 10^9 tokens
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity using SAE features.
rows.value: Mixed-language proportion rose again while high monosemanticity was maintained.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as the emergence of bilingual semantic representations.
rows.check: Bilingual-feature emergence is about cross-lingual alignment, not superposition or SAE recoverability.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: early to mid training, ≤ 4 × 10^9 tokens
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language feature proportion across layers.
rows.value: All layers showed a decrease in mixed-language proportion.
rows.note: The prose reports the trend across all layers.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: early to mid training, ≤ 4 × 10^9 tokens
rows.operation_detail: Measured monosemanticity across layers.
rows.value: All layers showed an increase in monosemanticity.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as initial learning of semantics within each language.
rows.check: Layer-wise monosemanticity of SAE features; no comparison to neurons or test of superposition.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: late training
rows.operation_detail: Compared mixed-language proportion and monosemanticity across layer groups.
rows.value: Mid layers followed the 14th-layer pattern of increasing bilingual alignment.
rows.note: The paper describes mid layers as especially capturing bilingual alignments.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: late training
rows.operation_detail: Compared mixed-language proportion and monosemanticity across layer groups.
rows.value: Mixed-language proportion increased and monosemanticity decreased compared with mid layers; the authors describe a tendency toward polysemanticity.
rows.note: The authors attribute this pattern partly to lower layers needing to distinguish a vocabulary of approximately 100,000 tokens, which exceeds the SAE intermediate dimension n.
rows.check: The lower-layer 'polysemanticity' refers to SAE features, not neurons. The vocabulary-exceeds-n explanation is authors' speculation, not a capacity test. The 'partial' state had no version referent.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 3.7B
rows.stage_stated: late training
rows.operation_detail: Compared mixed-language proportion, monosemanticity, and span length across layer groups.
rows.measure: Mixed-language proportion, monosemanticity, and span length
rows.value: Upper layers maintained a lower mixed-language proportion than mid layers; monosemanticity declined further, while features increasingly focused on longer spans.
rows.note: The authors explain the lower token-level monosemanticity as features capturing multi-token, contextually connected spans.
rows.check: Upper-layer span length and monosemanticity; different construct. The 'partial' state had no version referent.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 150M
rows.stage_stated: late training
rows.operation_detail: Compared mixed-language feature proportion and monosemanticity across layers and training stages.
rows.baseline: Early to mid training; comparison with larger models
rows.value: The late-stage increase in mixed-language proportion was smaller than in larger models, and features were less inclined to exhibit high monosemanticity across languages.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as a lower capacity for learning bilingual features than in larger models.
rows.check: Size comparison of bilingual alignment; different construct.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 150M
rows.stage_stated: late training
rows.operation_detail: Compared monosemanticity and span length in upper layers.
rows.value: Monosemanticity was smaller than in larger models, and the increase in span length was also smaller.
rows.note: The authors infer that upper layers in smaller models capture context-level meanings less effectively.
rows.check: Size comparison of upper-layer span and monosemanticity; different construct.

rows.subject: LLM-jp 150M
rows.stage_stated: all training phases
rows.operation_detail: Measured mixed-language proportion and monosemanticity in lower layers.
rows.value: The smaller model retained a relatively high mixed-language proportion and low monosemanticity; the authors describe this as inadequate semantic capture even within individual languages.
rows.note: The prose gives the comparison with the larger model.
rows.check: Size comparison of lower-layer language mix; different construct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The SAE analysis identifies features with changing language and semantic activation patterns, including coherent language-specific and later bilingual features (R1–R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Feature properties differ by layer: lower layers show a polysemantic tendency, while upper layers increasingly capture longer spans rather than token-level monosemanticity (R7–R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The smaller model shows weaker late-stage bilingual alignment and weaker upper-layer semantic/span development than larger models (R9–R11).
